findings.passage: His answer to fear is to get his hands on the controls. He says nothing there about how failure would look.
findings.problem: The hinge quotation is cut on both sides in a way that removes the Type 3 half. Reopened S02: the answer runs "it drives us. It drives me to work very hard. It drives me to make sure that my life is orderly, that I'm in control of my company..." and ends "Whenever I feel even remotely close to being at risk of failure, I can't stop working." His first and last answer to fear is overwork, which the evidence record itself (C08) calls a Three's answer. The draft shows only the middle sentence and then says his answer is the controls. The FAQ repeats the trimmed version.
findings.acceptance_test: The article reports the work sentences that sit before and after the block quote and says plainly that overwork fits Type 3. Any claim that the control clause is the discriminator is argued with those sentences visible. The 'Type 3 or Type 8' FAQ answer matches the corrected passage.

findings.passage: He named two routes to earned love, charm or achievement, without saying which was his.
findings.problem: The source does not support this discount. Reopened S03: "Depending on how you adapt, you can get very good at trying to earn the love of others. Bill Clinton is like me in that regard." That is first person, applied to himself. The next question is "Do the achievements fill the void?" and he answers "Yes and no," accepting the void as his, then tells the sister story as his answer. So the 'respected' telling in the opening was given as a reply about whether achievement fills a lack of love, which is Type 3 context the draft never mentions. 'Leading question' and 'second person' are also applied only to the adverse quote; the fear-of-failure answer was prompted too, and the control line comes from a prepared speech.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence is removed or rewritten to say he applied the earned-love description to himself ("like me in that regard") and answered "Yes and no" when asked if achievements fill the void. The article states, at the opening or in the Type 3 section, that the Playboy sister story was his answer to that question. Context discounts are applied to Type 8 self-reports by the same rule or dropped.

findings.passage: Across four decades, though, the thing these choices reliably cost him is approval, and he keeps paying.
findings.problem: This is the discriminator and it is asserted, not shown. (a) No source shows approval lost with an audience he cared about. In June 2000 Microsoft was the industry's villain; S08 says the probe unveiled Microsoft's front groups and S03 has him saying the investigators found the link and Oracle gave it to the media. (b) His own account says nonconformity paid: the 'magic in business' line the draft quotes continues, "The only way you can succeed in business big-time is to find places where conventional wisdom is wrong." That is a winning method, not a price. (c) The three episodes run 1997 to 2010, not four decades. (d) None of them trades approval for control. They show a man who does not back down. The thesis sentence and the first FAQ ("When approval and control conflict, he repeatedly takes control and absorbs the disapproval") describe a trade the episodes do not contain.
findings.acceptance_test: For each episode kept as evidence, the article cites who disapproved and what it cost him, or it says the cost is inferred. It addresses his own statement that nonconformity is how you win. The time span matches the episodes cited. The thesis sentence, the 60-word answer and the first FAQ either name the control gained in each case or are restated as what the record shows (he does not retreat under criticism), with confidence set to match.

findings.passage: He could look better or concede nothing, and he conceded nothing.
findings.problem: The section contradicts itself and the sources. One paragraph earlier the draft says "he conceded the unsavory part himself," quoting "Unsavory, yucky—kind of. But legal." The setup line "Ellison could have blamed the contractor" also sits badly with his own words in S03, quoted in the same section: "I didn't know they were going to go through Bill's garbage." He did put the method on the investigators while defending the purpose. S08 reports the garbage offer as a joke ("he joked"). The flagship episode is summarized more starkly than the record allows.
findings.acceptance_test: The summary says what the sources show: he denied knowing the method, called it unsavory but legal, and defended the purpose without apology. 'Conceded nothing' and the blame-the-contractor counterfactual are removed or supported by a source. The two adjacent paragraphs no longer disagree.

findings.passage: Nobody in the Academy of Achievement interview had asked about Michael Milken, who had served prison time for securities violations. Ellison brought him up anyway.
findings.problem: Two problems. First, a material fact is missing. Wikipedia's Knowledge Universe article (a lead, not in the evidence record, checked 2026-11-12) says Ellison was the third founder of that company with Michael and Lowell Milken in 1996 and put in $250 million. If that holds, the May 1997 remark defended a current business partner, which is much more than the draft's caveat that Milken was 'a wealthy, well-connected ally,' and it undercuts C17's inference that the remark 'gains nothing obvious.' Second, S02 is an edited interview, so what was or was not asked cannot be known. In the transcript the remark comes inside a list of famous people celebrity let him meet, straight after Walter Cronkite.
findings.acceptance_test: A reliable source on Knowledge Universe is opened and added to the record. If confirmed, the bullet states the 1996 partnership and the episode is no longer counted as approval given up for nothing; if it cannot be confirmed, the article says so. 'Nobody ... had asked' is replaced with what the transcript shows: he raised Milken while listing people he had met.

findings.passage: It is the trash press conference at a different scale: a public doubt about his word, answered with force and no explanation.
findings.problem: The cited source describes the opposite kind of move. Reopened S20: the Warner Bros. Discovery board objected that the money sat in a "revocable family trust"; the filing "was designed to silence those doubts," and the company statement spells out the terms, including a promise "not to revoke the Ellison family trust." The doubt was about a trust structure, not his word. An explanation was given. And he supplied exactly what the other side's board said was missing in order to win a deal. In 2000 he refused what critics wanted. In 2025 he met a counterparty's condition. The section heading ('the same move with a bigger number') rests on this analogy, and C26 is listed as type evidence.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph describes the guarantee as an answer to the board's stated objection about a revocable trust, attributed to the company statement. The trash-conference analogy and 'no explanation' are cut unless a source supports them. The guarantee is not presented as approval traded for control unless the article shows what approval he gave up; the heading is changed if the analogy goes.

findings.passage: it shows the same reflex as the public ones: quick, large, unhedged backing for someone inside his circle.
findings.problem: The draft's own source contradicts 'unhedged.' Reopened S16: after Ellison offered "whatever you recommend," Musk "proposed that Ellison offer $2 billion 'or more'," and "Ellison eventually settled on $1 billion." He put in half the recommended figure. The draft omits the recommendation. The same article shows Musk rationing access to the deal (to Reid Hoffman: "There is plenty of financial support ... you'd get priority"), so this was a sought-after allocation, not loyalty at a cost. The record also warns that outlets quote these texts differently.
findings.acceptance_test: The paragraph reports Musk's $2 billion-or-more recommendation and the $1 billion outcome. 'Unhedged' is deleted. The exchange is used as type evidence only if the article shows a cost or risk he accepted; otherwise it is reported as a fact. Wording is taken from the court exhibit or attributed to Fortune's summary.

findings.passage: He does not say he wanted to be rich, or first, or famous.
findings.problem: True of the two founding accounts, but the article's Type 3 case leaves out the strongest non-self-report evidence in sources it opened. S07, two sentences before the 'Rosebud' line the draft closes on, says of passing Bill Gates as the world's richest man: "To some who know him well, this goal may matter even more to Ellison than his company's becoming the dominant software player on the Net." S03 has him correcting Mallory: "It was because he wondered if he could be the first." S04 frames the PeopleSoft bid as a drive to be No. 1. The evidence record's own 'against' field lists the race with Gates for rank and wealth. The draft mentions the Gates rivalry only as scenery that both types share.
findings.acceptance_test: The 'Why not Type 3?' section includes the Fortune sentence about the wealth rank, attributed and dated, plus at least one of the 'first' or 'No. 1' statements, and says how the Type 8 reading handles them or that it does not. The quoted sentence is limited to what he said about founding the company.

findings.passage: "I wasn't a very good CEO," he said of Oracle's near-collapse in the early 1990s.
findings.problem: Adverse evidence from an opened source is used only to flatter. S27 says Oracle's staff "habitually overstated revenues," that the company posted its first losses in 1990, and that its market value fell 80 percent. The draft uses the episode once, as proof that he concedes fault easily, and never says what the fault was. The section on what the control costs other people quotes Ray Lane on a win-at-any-cost sales culture but does not connect it to the one documented time that culture nearly sank the company. Whether regulators or shareholders acted over the overstated revenue was not researched, so the controversy list may be incomplete.
findings.acceptance_test: The cost section states what happened in 1990 in plain terms with a source (overstated revenue, first loss, the fall in value). Research checks for regulatory action or shareholder suits over that accounting and adds any found, with outcome labels, to the article and the controversy registry. The concession quote stays beside the facts it concedes.

findings.passage: He called himself "a lifelong Democrat" in 2002.
findings.problem: The quotation stops at a 'but.' Reopened S03: "I was a big fan of Bill Clinton's and I'm happy with the current administration. I'm a lifelong Democrat, but I was not a supporter of Al Gore." He adds that he met George W. Bush "when I was deciding who I would support." The draft uses the fragment to set up the 2020 Trump fundraiser, which makes the later politics look like a sharper turn than his own 2002 words support.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence gives the full statement, including that he did not support Gore and was happy with the Bush administration, or the fragment is cut.

findings.passage: That reading accounts for 22 years of consistency. It does not answer the civil-liberties objection.
findings.problem: The rival explanation accounts for the consistency at least as well and for longer, and the draft leaves out the fact that shows it. S27 says the company's first contract was a database for the CIA and that 'Oracle' was that project's code name. The government was his founding customer, not only 'a key market.' Separately, the 2024 quotation is clipped: in S19 the sentence before it is "Every police officer is going to be supervised at all times, and if there's a problem, AI will report that problem." He was describing watching the police as well as citizens, which the heading about wanting more cameras flattens.
findings.acceptance_test: The section states the CIA founding contract with its source and says the commercial reading covers the whole period. The 2024 quotation includes the sentence about police being supervised. The type reading is offered as one account beside the commercial one, not as the one that 'accounts for' the record.

protected_passages.passage: Admired in one telling, respected in the other. It could be a slip of memory forty years on. It is also the open question about him.
protected_passages.reason: Both wordings check out against CBS and Playboy. The hook is specific to him, admits the innocent explanation, and sets up the real question without deciding it.

protected_passages.passage: That is one side of a relationship, told as a joke decades later. Louis Ellison's side is not on the record, so it stays a story Ellison tells and not a proven cause.
protected_passages.reason: Refuses the easy childhood-wound story at the exact point most profiles reach for it.

protected_passages.passage: None of this is conclusive. Grove knew him, and his remark is the best outside evidence that the persona is managed.
protected_passages.reason: States the best evidence against the article's own thesis in plain words and gives it weight.

protected_passages.passage: An Eight at ease can be gentle, so some of this fits. A six-year-old afraid his mother will not come home fits every type equally. It is better left unexplained.
protected_passages.reason: Declines to bend the type to cover a detail it cannot explain. Rare and worth keeping.

protected_passages.passage: The conviction concerned the forged email. It did not rule on everything about a relationship between a chief executive and an employee, and the available accounts tell the story mostly from Oracle's side.
protected_passages.reason: States the limit of the court outcome and of the sources without vouching for either party.

assessment: This draft confronts more adverse evidence than most: it gives Type 3 a real section, labels the unread biographies, states each controversy with an outcome and a response, and keeps a section for what the type cannot explain. The weakness is in the Type 8 case itself. I reopened S02, S03, S04, S05, S07, S08, S11, S14, S16, S19, S20 and S27 on 2026-11-12. Quotations are accurate as worded, but in the passages that carry the argument the surrounding text cuts against the reading and was left out: the fear-of-failure answer begins and ends with overwork (critic-01), the 'void' answer is first person and frames the sister story (critic-02), the garbage episode includes a concession and a disclaimer of the method (critic-04), the $40.4 billion guarantee met a counterparty's stated condition (critic-06), and the Musk commitment was half the recommended sum (critic-07). The Milken remark may have defended a business partner; that lead comes from Wikipedia and needs a proper source (critic-05). The claim that his defiance 'reliably cost him approval' has no evidence of the cost and runs against his own statement that nonconformity was 'magic in business' (critic-03). The Type 3 case omits the wealth-rank evidence in Fortune (critic-08), and the 1990 revenue overstatement appears only as proof of humility (critic-09). Context discounts are applied to the Type 3 quotes and not to the Type 8 ones. After these repairs the supported pattern is narrower: he does not retreat under criticism, and he names control as a motive in three self-reports. That may still favor Type 8 over Type 3 at medium confidence, but the 'approval versus control' trade as now worded is not shown. If the repair changes the discriminator or the confidence, the standard's hold for a fresh expanded review applies. Not checked by me: S09, S10, S12, S13, S15, S17, S18, S21 to S25, and the 2026 court status. Similarity advisory did not trip (maximum 0.024, at the noise ceiling, no shared phrases); the listed pairs are unrelated sentences and I found no reused argument.
